item.title: Whole blood transfusion in adult patients with traumatic brain injury: A systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Whole blood (WB) transfusion may improve outcomes in trauma patients compared with component therapy, but evidence in traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains limited. We evaluated the clinical effectiveness of WB transfusion in adults with TBI requiring transfusion.

Methods: We searched PubMed, Cochrane CENTRAL, CINAHL, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP for studies published from January 2006 through August 31, 2026. Eligible studies included randomized trials and observational studies using propensity score matching or inverse probability of treatment weighting. Random-effects meta-analysis with Hartung-Knapp adjustment was performed for mortality. Component-specific transfusion requirements were summarized qualitatively.

Results: Five studies were included in the systematic review, and four studies were included in the mortality meta-analysis. WB transfusion was not clearly associated with lower mortality (RR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.62-1.16; P = 0.19; I2 = 48.3%), with a 95% prediction interval of 0.48-1.49. Sensitivity analyses using alternative effect-size conversion methods, baseline risks, effect measures, and mortality definitions yielded consistent results. In exploratory leave-one-out analyses, pooled RRs ranged from 0.74 to 0.91, with all 95% CIs including 1. Three studies contributed component-specific transfusion data; red blood cells and plasma requirements were generally lower with WB, although this may partly reflect substitution by WB itself. The certainty of evidence was very low.

Conclusions: Current evidence is insufficient to determine whether WB transfusion reduces mortality after TBI because of the limited number of studies, clinical and methodological heterogeneity, risk of bias, and imprecision. Further randomized trials in clearly defined TBI populations are needed.

Nagamura T, Taniguchi H, Utsumi S, Yamada K, Terayama T, Mukherjee K

item.title: Pediatric cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the emergency department: Factors associated with outcome
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Pediatric cardiac arrest is usually studied either before hospital arrival or after admission, although the emergency department (ED) team resuscitates both. We examined factors associated with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), recurrent arrest and mortality in an ED cohort including both out-of-hospital cardiac arrests (OHCA) and in-ED cardiac arrests.

Methods: Retrospective cohort of all 83 children who received cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) in a university pediatric ED over 14 years (January 2010-March 2024). The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge; multivariable logistic regression identified factors independently associated with ED mortality.

Results: Median age was 35 months; 54.2% occurred out of hospital. ROSC was achieved in 42.2% and 30.1% survived the ED phase, but 9.9% survived to discharge. Epinephrine given later than 2 min was independently associated with ED mortality among the 27 patients with documented timing (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 7.73; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.27-46.97). Beyond 20 min of CPR, each additional minute was associated with ED death (aOR 1.32; 95% CI 1.01-1.73). Recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED occurred in 42.9%, of whom 6.7% survived versus 38.9% without recurrence (p = 0.039). Survival did not differ by arrest location, initial rhythm or timing of advanced airway management.

Conclusion: Resuscitation in the ED restored spontaneous circulation in many children, but few survived to discharge. Time to first epinephrine was independently associated with ED mortality in this cohort, whereas prolonged resuscitation and recurrent arrest after ROSC in the ED identified children at very high risk.

item.title: Modified pneumonia risk score using lung ultrasound for the prediction of radiographic pneumonia in children
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: The diagnosis of pneumonia in children based on clinical findings is challenging. The Pneumonia Risk Score (PRS), a clinical prediction tool, estimates the risk of radiographic pneumonia. Most children are classified as moderate-risk and are recommended to undergo chest x-ray (CXR). We hypothesized that lung ultrasound (LUS) may add diagnostic value beyond the PRS for predicting radiographic pneumonia.

Methods: We studied a convenience sample of children 6 months to 18 years old enrolled in a prospective LUS registry who presented to the emergency department with acute respiratory complaints and underwent CXR and LUS. The primary outcome was radiographic pneumonia. Logistic regression included the five PRS clinical predictors, and LUS consolidation ≥1 cm with bronchograms was added to create the PRS + LUS model. We compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the PRS to the PRS + LUS, evaluated risk re-classifications, and proposed a novel diagnostic algorithm.

Results: Among 275 children, 58 (21%) had radiographic pneumonia. LUS consolidation was strongly associated with pneumonia (OR 28.68 [95% CI, 9.98 to 82.43]). The PRS + LUS demonstrated greater diagnostic accuracy than the PRS alone (AUC 0.85 [95% CI, 0.77 to 0.89] versus 0.70 [95% CI, 0.61 to 0.76]; P < 0.001). Using our proposed novel two-step diagnostic algorithm, the PRS + LUS was calculated for patients assigned a moderate-risk score by PRS, resulting in assigning an additional 120 (44%) patients a high- or low-risk score, decreasing the moderate-risk category.

Conclusion: Adding LUS to the PRS improves prediction of radiographic pneumonia and may reduce CXR use, particularly among patients with moderate risk.

item.title: Effect modification by arterial pH on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation and neurological outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythm: A multicenter registry study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Arterial pH on emergency department (ED) arrival predicts outcomes after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but its effect on the association between extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) and neurological outcomes is unclear. We evaluated this association in patients with an initial shockable rhythm and assessed whether pH modified it.

Methods: We retrospectively analyzed the Korean Cardiac Arrest Research Consortium registry. Adults with presumed cardiac-origin OHCA, an initial shockable rhythm, ED cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and arterial blood gas data measured after ED arrival were included. Exposure was ECPR initiated in the ED; the primary outcome was favorable neurological outcome at discharge (Cerebral Performance Category 1-2). Arterial pH was categorized as low (≤6.85), medium (>6.85 and <7.05), or high (≥7.05). Multivariable logistic regression assessed ECPR-by-pH interaction, with optimal 1:2 propensity score matching as a sensitivity analysis.

Results: Of 2183 patients, 213 (9.8%) received ECPR and 154 (7.1%) had a favorable neurological outcome. The association between ECPR and favorable outcome differed across pH categories (p for interaction = 0.004): adjusted odds ratio (aOR) 7.34 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.84-18.98) in the low-pH group, 2.07 (95% CI, 1.06-4.03) in the medium-pH group, and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.37-1.94) in the high-pH group. The propensity score-matched analysis showed a similar pattern (p for interaction = 0.036).

Conclusions: Initial arterial pH modified the association between ECPR and neurological outcome after OHCA with an initial shockable rhythm. The association was strongest at low pH and not observed at high pH. Arterial pH may inform ECPR evaluation but should not determine treatment thresholds.

item.title: Defining organized cardiac motion and cardiac standstill in cardiac arrest using point of care ultrasound: A Delphi study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Aim: There are no widely accepted definitions of organized cardiac motion (OCM) and cardiac standstill (CS) using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) during cardiac arrest. We aimed to define these terms and provide guidance on the clinical application of these findings.

Methods: Statements defining OCM and CS were developed by a steering committee of experts after a comprehensive literature review aided by a librarian. A diverse panel of 20 experts was convened. Using Delphi methodology, the panel came to a consensus on definitions of OCM and CS after three rounds of voting.

Results: The panelists voted on 64 total statements pertaining to OCM and CS in cardiac arrest: 29 defining OCM, 23 defining cardiac standstill, and 12 examining clinical implications of OCM and CS. We defined OCM as coordinated contraction with change in left ventricular chamber size. Coordinated contraction with any change of the right ventricle may also be used if visualization of the left ventricle was not possible. Ventricular fibrillation, agonal motion, and isolated valvular movement were deemed not consistent with OCM. Cardiac standstill was defined as including the absence of all cardiac motion or the presence of isolated valvular movement alone. The panel recommended that POCUS can guide cardiac arrest resuscitation, and that these definitions are applicable to pediatric patients and the prehospital setting.

Conclusion: The expert panelists established consensus definitions of OCM and CS during cardiac arrest. These definitions can guide further research into POCUS use during cardiac arrest and aid ongoing efforts to standardize its use.

item.title: Applications of intravenous magnesium Sulfate in the emergency department: A narrative review
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Intravenous (IV) magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) has a variety of indications within the emergency department (ED) with evidence for its use continuing to evolve. It is used for common presentations such as headache/migraine, arrhythmias, severe respiratory exacerbations, and refractory hypokalemia while remaining the mainstay of treatment for preeclampsia/eclampsia. Evidence also supports its use for the management of shivering during targeted temperature management and a potential role for analgesia.

Objective: The focus of this review is to provide an update on the literature regarding the use of IV MgSO4 for common presentations in the ED for adults and provide an evidence-based approach to its utilization.

Discussion: The most robust trials suggest that IV MgSO4 serves a supporting role in the management of headache/migraine and may be used as an adjunct for rate control in patients with atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular rate. Magnesium sulfate should be reserved for patients experiencing severe respiratory exacerbations who fail to respond to initial therapy and may have a role in patients experiencing shivering during targeted temperature management. Routine empiric use in the management of hypokalemia is not suggested and evidence supporting its use for analgesia is limited. Intravenous MgSO4 remains first-line for preeclampsia/eclampsia and is the drug of choice in Torsades de Pointes. There was a low risk of adverse events across all studies evaluated with no serious events reported.

Conclusion: Intravenous MgSO4 is an adjunct for a myriad of indications in the ED. Additional high-quality research is needed to identify patients who benefit most from IV MgSO4.

item.title: Tenecteplase for isolated central retinal artery occlusion secondary to internal carotid artery dissection: A case report
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) is a blinding neuro-ophthalmologic emergency. Internal carotid artery dissection (ICAD) is a rare but underrecognized etiology of CRAO, frequently missed at initial presentation due to absence of pathognomonic clinical signs. While early intravenous thrombolysis confers benefit in CRAO, evidence for tenecteplase (TNK) in ICAD-associated cases remains exceedingly sparse. A 44-year-old previously healthy woman presented with isolated acute left CRAO after routine jogging. Intravenous TNK (0.25 mg/kg) administered within 3 h of onset achieved complete visual recovery the next day. Cervicocephalic vascular imaging confirmed left ICAD. Six-month follow-up after dual antiplatelet therapy demonstrated favorable recanalization, stable visual function, and no cerebral or ocular ischemic events occurred. This case suggests that intravenous TNK thrombolysis within the therapeutic window can yield favorable visual outcomes and acceptable safety in patients with ICAD-associated CRAO. For patients with acute visual loss occurring after exercise, ICAD must be actively suspected. Prompt cervicocephalic vascular etiological assessment alongside emergency care, delivered via multidisciplinary stroke pathways for improved long-term prognosis.

item.title: Comparative safety, efficiency, and diagnostic accuracy of YEARS, PEGeD, age-adjusted D-dimer, and fixed D-dimer strategies for excluding pulmonary embolism in the emergency department: a systematic review and meta-analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: D-dimer-based strategies, including fixed D-dimer, age-adjusted D-dimer (AADD), YEARS, and pulmonary embolism graduated D-dimer (PEGeD), have been developed to exclude pulmonary embolism (PE). This systematic review and meta-analysis compared their diagnostic accuracy, safety, and efficiency in emergency department (ED) patients with suspected PE.

Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Cochrane Library were searched from inception to July 2026. Outcomes included diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) safety (diagnostic failure rate), and efficiency (imaging avoidance). Bivariate random-effects models were used in pooling diagnostic accuracy outcomes and imaging avoidance rates were expressed as percentages.

Results: Twenty-four studies involving 63,583 patients were included. The pooled analysis demonstrated a sensitivity of 98.3% (95% CI, 97.3 to 99.1), 96.5% (95% CI: 94.3 to 98.2), 91.8% (95% CI: 87.2 to 95.4), and 91.0% (95% CI: 79.5 to 95.9), and a pooled specificity of 22.0% (95% CI: 12.8 to 38.8), 34.7% (95% CI: 20.0 to 51.7), 51.6% (95% CI: 32.5 to 71.5), and 43.6 (95% CI: 23.0 to 69.5) for fixed D-dimer, AADD, YEARS, and PEGeD algorithm, respectively. Pooled imaging avoidance rates were 15% (95% CI: 0 to 42) for fixed D-dimer, 16% (95% CI: 0 to 45) for AADD, 51% (95% CI: 23 to 79) for YEARS, and 53% (95% CI: 25 to 81).

Conclusion: Across studies, all D-dimer strategies showed high pooled sensitivity, with variable specificity and imaging avoidance rates. Diagnostic failure rates were reported in a limited number of studies, limiting conclusions regarding clinical safety.

Shaban EE, Abosamak MF, Elmelliti H, Shaban A, Shaban A, Jobran AWM

item.title: Direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade in geriatric patients with multiple rib fractures and flail chest: A national analysis
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: It remains unclear whether direct ICU admission benefits geriatric patients compared with delayed floor-to-ICU upgrade. The study evaluated the association of direct ICU admission versus floor-to-ICU upgrade with clinical outcomes in geriatric trauma patients with flail chest and thoracic injury, stratified by oxygenation compromise, frailty, and rib fracture burden.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used the 2017-2024 ACS-TQIP-PUF to identify patients aged 65 years or older with blunt trauma, flail chest, at least three rib fractures, an Injury Severity Score of 9 or greater, and thoracic injury. Patients were classified as floor admission without ICU upgrade, direct ICU admission, or floor-to-ICU upgrade. The primary adjusted analysis compared direct ICU admission with floor-to-ICU upgrade, using floor-to-ICU upgrade as the reference group.

Results: A total of 6743 patients were included. Mortality did not differ significantly between direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade in the primary adjusted analysis (aOR 0.732, 95% CI 0.467-1.148, p = 0.174). Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation (aOR 0.355, 95% CI 0.251-0.502, p < 0.001), ARDS (aOR 0.412, 95% CI 0.172-0.987, p = 0.047), sepsis (aOR 0.352, 95% CI 0.171-0.725, p = 0.005), and DVT (aOR 0.444, 95% CI 0.209-0.942, p = 0.034). Mortality was lower with direct ICU admission among patients with 3-5 documented rib fractures (aOR 0.535, 95% CI 0.296-0.969, p = 0.039), and the association with fewer unplanned intubations persisted across all subgroups. In the secondary analysis, both direct ICU admission and floor-to-ICU upgrade were associated with higher mortality, lower odds of discharge home, and fewer ventilator-free days than floor admission without ICU upgrade.

Conclusion: Direct ICU admission was associated with lower odds of unplanned intubation, ARDS, sepsis, and DVT compared with floor-to-ICU upgrade. These findings support identifying at-risk geriatric rib fracture patients for direct ICU admission before deterioration occurs.

Nasef Y, Nishida C, Bundschu I, Hus A, Kumar S, Rogers L

item.title: Cost and operational impact of a molecular point-of-care test for sexually transmitted infections in the emergency department
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Female patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected sexually transmitted infections (STIs) have historically been evaluated using centralized laboratory testing (CLT), with results unavailable during the visit. Point-of-care (POC) tests enable real-time diagnosis but have higher direct costs than CLT.

Objective: To compare hospital and societal costs of CLT and POC STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomonas) among female ED patients with suspected infection, and to assess effects on underdiagnosis, overtreatment, undertreatment, and ED recidivism.

Design: Decision analysis through cost tables using data from a pre-post implementation study.

Setting: Large urban academic ED (Johns Hopkins Hospital).

Interventions: CLT (nucleic acid amplification test [NAAT]/wet preparation) versus molecular POC STI testing.

Measurements: Direct testing costs, follow-up costs for informing patients after discharge, costs of overtreatment/undertreatment, and ED return visits within 30 days. Analyses were conducted from hospital and societal perspectives over 12-month horizon.

Results: Direct POC testing costs for 1000 women exceeded CLT by $16,502. This difference was not offset by lower follow-up costs for undertreatment or by societal costs of under- or overtreatment. From the hospital perspective, costs may be offset by increased margins from maximizing ED Examination room utilization. Threshold analysis shows room time need not be fully occupied, nor margins equal full revenue, to achieve net revenue gain.

Conclusions: POC testing for STIs, given current pricing and unchanged reimbursement, increases societal costs and reduces hospital revenue versus CLT. However, EDs and hospitals may increase net revenue, by improved patient throughput thereby generating revenue if ED wait times are long.

Paul-Ledesma A, Dashler G, Hsieh YH, Maliszewski K, Saheed M, Mann E

item.title: Predicting survival in pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: Development and internal validation of risk scores
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) in the pediatric population is associated with poor survival and neurological outcomes. We aimed to develop and internally validate risk scores to predict survival to discharge in pediatric OHCA patients.

Methods: We included pediatric OHCA patients in the Cardiac Arrest Registry to Enhance Survival from 2013 to 2023. We used logistic regression (LR) and classification and regression trees (CART) to develop risk scores using 70% of the data and validated them using the remaining 30% of the data. We used discrimination and predictive accuracy to evaluate model performance.

Results: We included 26,895 pediatric patients, of whom 27.8% survived to hospital admission and 11.9% survived to hospital discharge. We developed three separate risk scores for i) infants ii) preschool and school-age children, and iii) adolescents. The most important predictor variables were gender, arrest location, witness status, etiology of arrest, bystander CPR, use of prehospital AED, and first rhythm. Models developed using both LR and CART approaches had good classification accuracy (AUROCC for LR: 0.81, 0.77 and 0.82, AUROCC for CART: 0.78, 0.76, 0.82 for the three age groups) However, we found CART models to be the most useful because they are simpler to follow, classified more patients in low and high survival categories using a smaller number of predictors. The average survival probability in infants for each risk group was 3%, 13%, and 33%, for preschool and school-age children it was 4%, 11%, and 29%, whereas for adolescents it was 4%, 13%, and 48% for the low, moderate, and high survival categories.

Conclusion: Pediatric patients experiencing OHCA can be classified into low, moderate, and high survival categories using a simple risk score and easily identified prehospital variables. These risk scores can facilitate research, monitor the quality of medical services and can potentially support clinical decision-making.

Mawani M, McNally B, Knight J, Shen Y, Ebell M

item.title: Integration of multimodal large language models into point-of-care ultrasound documentation: A pilot study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Introduction: There are no studies evaluating the potential to deploy artificial intelligence in the interpretation of cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) documentation. Telexy Health developed an image interpretation and documentation system using multimodal model extensions with video capabilities (MLLM) and deployed it on the POCUS manager QpathE. This study evaluated the MLLM's agreement to experts in identifying cardiac POCUS views and interpreting normal and abnormal examinations.

Methods: This was a retrospective pilot study using cardiac POCUS studies stored in QPathE. The MLLM was applied to POCUS examinations until 350 examinations were reached, 100 normal, and 250 with pathology. MLLM view identification and interpretation were recorded using Qualtrics, with expert image review serving as the gold standard.

Results: The MLLM was applied to 370 examinations, with 20 failures. View identification agreed with expert review in 151 examinations (43.1%). Cohen's kappa showed fair agreement for apical four-chamber views between expert and MLLM, with moderate agreement for parasternal long axis, parasternal short axis, subxiphoid, and inferior vena cava views. The MLLM agreed with expert interpretation 86 of 100 normal examinations; the agreement varied by pathology with pericardial effusion, ejection fraction, aortic outflow tract, chamber size, and inferior vena cava having an agreement of 8%, 4%, 70%, 0%, and 12% respectively.

Conclusion: While agreement in image interpretation was poor, this vendor agnostic workflow demonstrated the ability to integrate an MLLM model into image interpretation. While it should not be incorporated into clinical practice in this state, future model improvement may enable automated POCUS interpretation and documentation.

Boivin Z, Jaffa E, Agaraj I, Danta M, Park GY, Liu RB
